summary: Mission Nova: Europa Deep is a free browser game where players design, manage and simulate a complete mission to the ocean beneath Europa's ice. Players choose a launch vehicle, radiation protection, a power source and up to three instruments. Live telemetry tracks budget ($5.2B cap), probe mass, power at arrival and shielding. An on-board co-pilot, E.V.A., explains every failed check so players can fix the design and try again. They then fly to Jupiter, melt through a 29 km ice shell, respond to an ocean event using only the tools they packed, and decide how much data to send home with the power they have left. The game turns abstract engineering trade-offs (cost vs. speed, mass vs. power, instruments vs. budget) into decisions students feel straight away. Key values come from NASA and JPL documents. Every number is tagged as NASA data, secondary source, derived value or game assumption, which teaches students to tell evidence from assumption.
details:
What it does:

Players act as mission engineers in four steps.

(1) Design: pick Falcon Heavy or SLS Block 1B, one of four radiation-protection options, a power source (solar, 6× MMRTG, 5× eMMRTG, or Kilopower), and the ice-melting drill plus up to two tools (submarine science payload, sonar, camera).

(2) Check & Launch: five checks must pass (cost ≤ $5.2B, mass within the launcher's allowance, power at arrival ≥ need, shielding level 3+, drill on board), and E.V.A. explains each failure in plain language.

(3) Launch, land, and descend: the animated trajectory and melt-through use the transit time of the chosen launcher (5.5 or 2.7 years). Radioisotope power decays during the trip, so a slower route means less power on arrival.

(4) Explore and transmit: a random ocean event (plume or faint lights) can only be studied with tools on board. Sending the full dataset needs 50 W of spare power; otherwise, a 60% summary is sent. A report shows the score, and "Improve This Design" lets players iterate.

Benefits and impact:

Students experience a whole mission from concept to operation in about ten minutes. Each challenge trade-off (objectives, design, instruments, launch vehicles, budget, power, mass, communications, and orbital route) is a real decision with consequences.

Tools:

HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript with Canvas animation. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, needs no installs, and works offline on school devices.

Creativity:

An AI co-pilot gives hints, power decay is physically modeled using NASA's MMRTG figures, and every value carries a source tag (N/S/D/A).

Factors considered:

Accessibility (keyboard focus, ARIA labels, readable contrast), low device requirements, scientific honesty (game assumptions are labeled because no Europa cryobot has flown), and a budget cap based on Europa Clipper.
